```{python}
#| include: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from statsforecast import StatsForecast
from statsforecast.models import (HistoricAverage, Naive, RandomWalkWithDrift,
                                  SeasonalNaive)
from utilsforecast.losses import mae, mape, mase, rmse, rmsse

from coursekit import datasets as D
from coursekit import plotting as P

P.use_course_style()

spine = D.spine()
H = 24
train, test = D.train_test(spine, h=H)

MODELS = ["HistoricAverage", "Naive", "SeasonalNaive", "RWD"]
LABELS = {"HistoricAverage": "Mean", "Naive": "Naive",
          "SeasonalNaive": "Seasonal naive", "RWD": "Drift"}

sf = StatsForecast(
    models=[HistoricAverage(), Naive(), SeasonalNaive(season_length=12),
            RandomWalkWithDrift()],
    freq=D.FREQ, n_jobs=1,
)
fc = sf.forecast(df=train, h=H, level=[80])
merged = test.merge(fc, on=["unique_id", "ds"])

# Rolling-origin cross-validation: 8 origins, one year forecast each.
N_WINDOWS, CV_H = 8, 12
cv = sf.cross_validation(df=spine, h=CV_H, step_size=CV_H,
                         n_windows=N_WINDOWS, level=[80])

per_window = pd.DataFrame([
    mase(g.drop(columns=["cutoff"]), models=MODELS, seasonality=12,
         train_df=spine[spine["ds"] <= cut])[MODELS].iloc[0]
    for cut, g in cv.groupby("cutoff")
]).reset_index(drop=True)

coverage = {m: float(((cv["y"] >= cv[f"{m}-lo-80"])
                      & (cv["y"] <= cv[f"{m}-hi-80"])).mean()) for m in MODELS}
```

# A. Scoring a point forecast {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #00C9A7)"}

Ch 5.8 · Point forecast metrics

## Error metric summary

Forecast error: $e_{T+h} = y_{T+h} - \hat{y}_{T+h|T}$

| Metric | Property | Limitation |
|---|---|---|
| **MAE** | Easy to interpret | Scale-dependent (cannot compare across series) |
| **RMSE** | Penalizes large errors | Scale-dependent |
| **MAPE** | Percentage error | Explodes near zero; asymmetric |
| **MASE** | **Scale-free** (relative to baseline) | Requires seasonal period |

::: {.notes}
MAE and RMSE work well within a single series. To compare across different products or series, use MASE.
:::

## The flaw with MAPE

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n = 48
low = pd.DataFrame({
    "unique_id": "spare parts",
    "ds": pd.date_range("2020-01-01", periods=n, freq="MS"),
    "y": np.clip(rng.poisson(1.4, n).astype(float), 0.2, None),
})
pred_hi = low["y"] + 2.0
pred_lo = low["y"] - 0.15

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.6))
ax.plot(low["ds"], low["y"], color=P.BLACK, lw=1.2, label="Actual (Low Volume)")
ax.plot(low["ds"], pred_hi, color=P.ORANGE, lw=1.4, label="Forecast A (+2.0)")
ax.plot(low["ds"], pred_lo, color=P.BLUE, lw=1.4, label="Forecast B (-0.15)")
ax.set(title="Low-Volume Demand Breaks MAPE")
ax.legend(frameon=False, ncols=3)
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: Simulated low-volume / intermittent demand series (Poisson)
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n = 48
low = pd.DataFrame({
    "unique_id": "spare parts",
    "ds": pd.date_range("2020-01-01", periods=n, freq="MS"),
    "y": np.clip(rng.poisson(1.4, n).astype(float), 0.2, None),
})
pred_hi = low["y"] + 2.0
pred_lo = low["y"] - 0.15

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.6))
ax.plot(low["ds"], low["y"], color=P.BLACK, lw=1.2, label="Actual (Low Volume)")
ax.plot(low["ds"], pred_hi, color=P.ORANGE, lw=1.4, label="Forecast A (+2.0)")
ax.plot(low["ds"], pred_lo, color=P.BLUE, lw=1.4, label="Forecast B (-0.15)")
```

:::

::: {.incremental}
- Forecast A: MAE = 2.00, MAPE = **184%**
- Forecast B: MAE = 0.15, MAPE = **23%**
:::

## 3 reasons to avoid MAPE for model selection

::: {.incremental}
1. **Undefined at zero** — explodes on intermittent / low-volume demand
2. **Asymmetric** — penalizes over-forecasting far more than under-forecasting
3. **Fails without a true zero** — invalid for temperature (°C)
:::

. . .

::: {.cardbox}
Report MAPE to executives if required, but **never optimize models using MAPE**.
:::

## Scaled Errors: MASE

Error divided by the in-sample Seasonal Naive error ($Q$):

$$\text{MASE} = \frac{\text{MAE}}{Q}$$

. . .

::: {.incremental}
- **$\text{MASE} < 1$** $\rightarrow$ **Better** than the seasonal naive baseline
- **$\text{MASE} = 1$** $\rightarrow$ Exactly as good as seasonal naive
- **$\text{MASE} > 1$** $\rightarrow$ **Worse** than simple baseline
:::

## Benchmarks scored on test set

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
scores = pd.DataFrame({
    "MAE": mae(merged, models=MODELS)[MODELS].iloc[0],
    "RMSE": rmse(merged, models=MODELS)[MODELS].iloc[0],
    "MAPE %": mape(merged, models=MODELS)[MODELS].iloc[0] * 100,
    "MASE": mase(merged, models=MODELS, seasonality=12, train_df=train)[MODELS].iloc[0],
    "RMSSE": rmsse(merged, models=MODELS, seasonality=12, train_df=train)[MODELS].iloc[0],
})
scores.index = [LABELS[m] for m in scores.index]
print(scores.round(2).to_string())
```

::: {.cardbox .teal}
Seasonal Naive wins across all metrics ($\text{MASE} = 1.11$).
:::

::: {.notes}
MASE > 1.0 because forecasting 24 months ahead is harder than in-sample 1-step naive errors.
:::

# B. One split is not evidence {.sdaia-dark background-gradient="linear-gradient(135deg, #1C355E, #FF7A5C)"}

Ch 5.10 · Rolling-origin cross-validation

## Why a single train/test split fails

::: {.incremental}
- A single 24-month split is just **one sample point**
- Score depends heavily on economic conditions during that window
- High variance ($\pm 16\%$ error bars on 24 observations)
- Encourages data snooping and overfitting
:::

. . .

::: {.cardbox .navy}
Time series cannot use standard k-fold. We need **rolling origins**.
:::

## Rolling-Origin Cross-Validation

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.4))
P.cv_staircase(n_obs=96, initial=48, horizon=12, step=12, ax=ax,
               title="Expanding Training Window Across Origins")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Diagram: Rolling-origin cross-validation splits (expanding window)
# 96 total periods, initial train size 48, horizon 12, step size 12
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.4))
P.cv_staircase(n_obs=96, initial=48, horizon=12, step=12, ax=ax,
               title="Expanding Training Window Across Origins")
```

:::

::: {.cardbox .teal}
Each fold trains only on past data. **No fold ever peeks into its future**.
:::

## Key CV parameters

```python
# Cross-validation setup with StatsForecast on Victorian takeaway turnover (spine):
cv = sf.cross_validation(
    df=spine,
    h=12,          # Forecast horizon matched to business need
    step_size=12,  # Steps between successive origins
    n_windows=8,   # Number of evaluation folds
    level=[80],
)
```

::: {.incremental}
- **`h`** — match the true operational planning horizon
- **`step_size`** — frequency of forecast production
- **`n_windows`** — number of independent test origins
:::

## Cross-validation results across 8 folds

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.0))

single = mase(merged, models=MODELS, seasonality=12, train_df=train)[MODELS].iloc[0]
x = np.arange(len(MODELS))
axes[0].bar(x - 0.2, single.values, width=0.4, color=P.GREY, label="Single Split")
axes[0].bar(x + 0.2, per_window.mean().values, width=0.4, color=P.BLUE,
            label=f"Mean of {N_WINDOWS} Folds")
axes[0].set_xticks(x, [LABELS[m] for m in MODELS], rotation=20, ha="right")
axes[0].set(ylabel="MASE", title="Model Ranking is Stable")
axes[0].legend(frameon=False)

for i, m in enumerate(MODELS):
    axes[1].scatter(np.full(len(per_window), i), per_window[m], s=40,
                    color=P.ORANGE, alpha=0.75, zorder=3)
axes[1].set_xticks(range(len(MODELS)), [LABELS[m] for m in MODELS],
                   rotation=20, ha="right")
axes[1].set(ylabel="MASE", title="Score Distribution across Folds")
axes[1].set_yscale("log")
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: Victorian takeaway food turnover (cv = sf.cross_validation(spine, n_windows=8))
# Left: Single 24-month split vs Mean across 8 CV origins
# Right: Distribution of MASE across individual CV folds
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4.0))

single = mase(merged, models=MODELS, seasonality=12, train_df=train)[MODELS].iloc[0]
x = np.arange(len(MODELS))
axes[0].bar(x - 0.2, single.values, width=0.4, color=P.GREY, label="Single Split")
axes[0].bar(x + 0.2, per_window.mean().values, width=0.4, color=P.BLUE, label=f"Mean of {N_WINDOWS} Folds")

for i, m in enumerate(MODELS):
    axes[1].scatter(np.full(len(per_window), i), per_window[m], s=40, color=P.ORANGE, alpha=0.75, zorder=3)
```

:::

::: {.notes}
Notice the right plot: for Seasonal Naive, individual fold MASE ranges from 0.71 to 1.90. The single split was lucky/unlucky, but the average is robust.
:::

## Interval coverage across all 8 folds

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot
```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.4))
names = [LABELS[m] for m in MODELS]
vals = [coverage[m] for m in MODELS]
cols = [P.BLUE if abs(v - 0.8) < 0.1 else P.ORANGE for v in vals]
ax.barh(names, vals, color=cols, height=0.6)
ax.axvline(0.8, color=P.BLACK, ls="--", lw=1.4)
ax.text(0.8, -0.75, " Nominal 80%", size=10)
for i, v in enumerate(vals):
    ax.text(v, i, f" {v:.0%}", va="center", size=10)
ax.set(xlim=(0, 1.05), title=f"80% Interval Coverage ({N_WINDOWS * CV_H} Scored Points)")
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.show()
```

### Code
```python
# Dataset: Victorian takeaway food turnover (cv across 8 origins x 12 horizon = 96 points)
# Coverage = percentage of holdout points falling between 80% lo/hi bounds
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.4))
names = [LABELS[m] for m in MODELS]
vals = [coverage[m] for m in MODELS]
cols = [P.BLUE if abs(v - 0.8) < 0.1 else P.ORANGE for v in vals]
ax.barh(names, vals, color=cols, height=0.6)
ax.axvline(0.8, color=P.BLACK, ls="--", lw=1.4)
```

:::

::: {.incremental}
- **Seasonal Naive**: 77% coverage (near nominal 80%)
- **Mean Model**: 0% coverage (fails on trending data)
:::

## Information leakage risks

```{dot}
//| fig-width: 9.5
digraph G {
    bgcolor="transparent";
    rankdir=LR;
    node [shape=box style="rounded,filled" fontname="Noto Sans" fontsize=12
          color="#1C355E" penwidth=2 margin="0.16,0.09"];
    edge [fontname="Noto Sans" fontsize=11 color="#5b6678" penwidth=1.6];

    A [label="Scaling / Normalizing\non the full series" fillcolor="#E96852" fontcolor="white"];
    B [label="Centered rolling\nwindow features" fillcolor="#E96852" fontcolor="white"];
    C [label="Tuning hyperparameters\non the test set" fillcolor="#E96852" fontcolor="white"];
    L [label="Data Leakage\nOver-optimistic CV,\npoor production" fillcolor="#1C355E" fontcolor="white"];

    A -> L; B -> L; C -> L;
}
```

::: {.notes}
Always fit scalers, imputers, and feature engineering strictly on each fold's training history.
:::

## Evaluation pitfalls to avoid

::: {.incremental}
- **Regime changes** — verify if old folds disagree with recent folds
- **Underpowered sample** — evaluate over sufficient origins ($>50$ points)
- **Overlapping folds** — beware overly narrow confidence intervals when `step_size < h`
- **Data gaps** — verify timestamp continuity across all origins
:::
